title: Sticks! Cudgels!

paragraphs: As I sit writing these notes of my life story, my state of mind today is restless. Neither the turbulence of the deep sea nor molten lava leaping and scattering from a volcano would be an adequate image for the pain in my heart.

Friends place garlands on me. They heap praise on me for giving good government. I shake hands with them. I smile. I converse warmly. Yet in all these actions there is no complete satisfaction even within myself. If I do not shake an extended hand, I fear they will be hurt. If I do not accept a garland, I fear they will think, "Is he so arrogant?" If I do not appear cheerful, I worry that people will spread the news, "Perhaps he has some illness he cannot speak of publicly." What a painful, absurd life!

To outward appearance: office, fame, praise. Imagine seating a man on a chair covered with a silk cushion, while needles hidden inside the cushion prick him all over, and the crowd in front cries, "Ah! Is he not Indra? Is he not Chandra?" Like a man who, fearing public opinion, endures the needle-pricks and smiles for form's sake while bleeding, I too smile today; I too appear happy. That is the benefit I receive from office!

Yet there was a time when I, who cannot bear these needle-point pricks, accepted spear-points with a smiling face. That was the nearly thirty years of opposition life up to the end of 1966. Spears have aimed at my chest. Stones have tested my head. Sticks, staffs and cudgels have tasted my body. Death has come close to me again and again, only to move away. There were some who regretted—not that it came close, but that it went away!

Whenever I faced those cruel events, however, I felt exhilaration. I did not suffer wounds of the mind. A warrior on the battlefield will be ready to offer his head to the sword that flies toward him. But if you ask that same warrior to lie down and roll on the nerunji thorns scattered through his own garden, could he bear it?

Among the gravest dangers that came to my head, one of the foremost was the danger in Puducherry. After finishing our movement-propaganda plays in Villupuram, we left for Puducherry—the soil where Aurobindo lived, the land where Bharathiyar wandered composing splendid poems to break the chains of slavery, the region where the self-respecting poet Bharathidasan, fearless of heart and rich in words, took up his pen.

It was a time when India was under the British and the Puducherry-Karaikal regions were under the French. On Puducherry's beautiful streets, French men and women moved about in colourful fashion. Come evening, men and women, intoxicated with drink, would travel through the bazaar streets in rickshaws pulled by Tamils, embracing and kissing one another. Puducherry's streets were beautiful and clean; yet what I saw as unbearable sights parading under the name of foreign civilization remained a great blemish on Puducherry.

Even six-year-old boys could be seen walking the streets smoking. There were plenty of policemen who would ask those children for a light for their beedis. On the Puducherry seafront stood, in imposing splendour, a statue of Dupleix—the man who had tried to conquer India, whose effort was checked by Clive, and whose French power remained over only a few small territories such as Puducherry, Karaikal, Mahe and Yanam.

In 1945, when India itself was in British hands and Puducherry, hanging from its neck like a pendant, was in French hands, our Dravidian Actors' Association began staging its plays at Keple Theatre. We did not meet the disappointment we had faced in Villupuram. Crowds came every day; many had to turn back for lack of space.

The play Santa, or Palaniyappan, in which I acted, ran for twenty-five consecutive days with excellent collections. My character in the play was named Sivaguru. The public in Puducherry began affectionately calling me "Sivaguru." Dravidar Kazhagam workers and frontline activists there gathered around me and gave me encouragement and enthusiasm.

With the support of Mr. Perumal, Kanchi Kalyanasundaram was running the weekly Thozhilalar Mithiran. That Perumal was the man known as Avukka Perumal, who for a time served as Speaker in Puducherry. In local usage there, avukka meant lawyer. The editor encouraged me to write articles for Thozhilalar Mithiran. If I kept up that duty, I could count on tea at his office all week.

That office was really a place meant for parking cars. Instead of a car, there was a typesetting space and the editor's chair. I wrote an article titled "That Pen!" It was about a pen that had gone missing from Gandhiji's ashram. The very next day after the issue appeared, the local Congress men had identified me. In the next issue I wrote another article, "What If Gandhi Became Viceroy?" They did not wait for me to write a third. One night they gathered in a grim house and drew up a conspiracy.

Just as their plan seemed likely to succeed, we unexpectedly decided to organize a movement conference in Puducherry and threw ourselves completely into the preparations. Drama work all night; conference work by day. Everything was completed as we wished for the conference to be held with dignity and splendour. Periyar, Arignar Anna, Alagirisami and other movement leaders took part.

The conference began at ten in the morning. Those who had planned to create trouble began gathering opposite the entrance—one, two, ten, a hundred—and shouting slogans of protest. Their cry was, "Dravidian leaders! Go back!" Anna began his speech by asking: "To call someone 'Come!' is Tamil culture. What reason is there to say 'Go!'?" He delivered a rare speech and then hoisted the movement flag.

The very next moment after the flag went up, the opponents pulled down the flagpole. That was enough: the commotion began. After sending Periyar, Anna and the other leaders away safely in vehicles and rickshaws, Bharathidasan, Kanchi Kalyanasundaram and I were walking along the street. Suddenly a large crowd surrounded the three of us.

The three of us were scattered in different directions. Someone took Bharathidasan away and hid him in a house. One of his shoes lay in the street. They used it as a weapon to beat me. It was a heavy hobnailed boot. There is no need to explain how such a blow felt. It hurt then. Yet even now, when I remember the incident, it tastes sweet.
